name: Differentiated Customer Value

positioning.oneLineSummary: Traces differentiated capability to a specific champion-relevant outcome and verifies that customers experience and value it.
positioning.productLabel: Differentiated-Value Lens — based on April Dunford's 2026 public materials
notAClaimOf: generic save-time or make-money claims being differentiated

attribution.display: Based on April Dunford's 2026 public materials

neutralParaphrase: For each differentiated capability, ask what outcome it enables for the champion and why that outcome matters compared with real alternatives. Require customer and operating proof; separate differentiated value from generic economic language, copywriting, other-stakeholder objections, and future promises.

locator.value: 03:14-17:23, capabilities, outcomes, repeated 'so what', champion, and objections
Expanded differentiated-value section in updated edition

requiredConditions: OA2-02 and OA2-03 have evidenced alternatives and differentiated capabilities.
Champion and buying context are defined.
Value outcomes can be observed or tested.

requiredEvidence.description: Capability, changed workflow or decision, intermediate outcome, business outcome, beneficiary, and alternative comparison.
Measured or independently corroborated time, quality, risk, revenue, cost, conversion, or strategic outcome.
Evidence the champion understands, prioritizes, and can mobilize the organization around the outcome.

decisionQuestions: What outcome does the differentiated capability enable?
Why is that outcome better than what real alternatives provide?
Does the champion care enough for the value to influence a purchase?
What measured result and counterexample support or challenge the chain?
positiveSignals: A capability-to-outcome chain is specific and customer verified.
The champion uses the outcome to justify purchase or expansion.
The outcome differs materially from alternatives.
Proof includes baselines, conditions, and unsuccessful cases.
redFlags: Value is a feature list or generic efficiency claim.
Management jumps from capability to revenue without a workflow mechanism.
Value is defined for every stakeholder simultaneously.
Objection handling or table stakes are presented as differentiated value.
disconfirmingEvidence: Customers like the feature but do not change behavior or budget.
Alternatives deliver the same outcome at acceptable cost.
Only the vendor, not the champion, articulates the value.
Measured outcomes disappear outside a curated case study.
contraindications: Do not calculate ROI from unverified assumptions.
Do not collapse champion value and stakeholder objections.
Do not accept copywriting as outcome evidence.

instructions: Trace each differentiated capability to a champion-relevant outcome.
Compare that outcome with real alternatives.
Review measured proof, baselines, and counterexamples.
Separate core value, table stakes, objections, and future promises.
Conclude demonstrated, emerging, generic, contradicted, or insufficient.

deterministicRule.prohibition: The language model must not calculate ROI or invent outcome baselines.

sourceReliability.high: Customer KPIs, telemetry, experiments, and win/loss converge.

evidenceStrength.high: Repeated differentiated outcome changes purchase or use behavior.

evidenceCoverage.high: Capability, alternative, mechanism, champion, baseline, outcome, and counterexamples covered.

applicabilityConfidence.high: Best-fit purchase decisions materially depend on the value.

empiricalQualifications: Customer value varies by segment and buying role.
Observed ROI can suffer selection bias.

rights.notes: Author's public 2026 guidance is neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Review licensed expanded value chapter and define minimum outcome proof.
